description: I'm Dens Akoka from Dundee, Scotland, joining Space Apps London. I make Pale Dot (paledot.org), a 3D journey from Earth to the edge of the universe, with planet sizes and distances at true scale. For this challenge I'll add guided tours of the machines NASA left behind: Apollo sites and rovers, Viking 1, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars, and Voyager 1 and 2 in interstellar space. Real NASA photos, landing sites pinned in 3D, and each machine's real flight path from NASA/JPL data.
summary: Left Behind tells the stories of NASA hardware inside Pale Dot, a true-scale 3D explorer running on a shared real-date simulation clock. Seven guided tours cover Apollo 11’s landing site and laser reflector, the Apollo 15–17 lunar rovers, Viking 1, Opportunity, Ingenuity, and Voyager 1 and 2. Students explore their journeys, discoveries and present-day status through dated views, archival photographs and credited sources. Cached NASA/JPL Horizons data supplies supported spacecraft trajectories; other journeys are explicitly labelled simplified paths. Published landing coordinates, orbital imagery and terrain data connect the stories to real places, while missing final-location data is acknowledged. The tours sit alongside Pale Dot’s original “Begin at Earth” journey. Voyager 1’s “One Last Look” combines an illustrative Sunward view with NASA’s archival photographs and a comparison of Earth’s tiny image size. A simulated signal race makes communication delay tangible. Designed for ages 11–18 and their teachers, Left Behind asks: what did we leave behind, and what did it teach us?
details:
What it does

Left Behind is a set of guided, explorable stories inside Pale Dot, a true-scale 3D journey from Earth to the edge of the observable universe. It introduces school-age space fans aged 11–18 and their teachers to NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space.

Seven guided tours cover the Apollo 11 landing site and its laser reflector; the Apollo 15, 16 and 17 Lunar Roving Vehicles together; Viking 1; Opportunity; Ingenuity; Voyager 2; and Voyager 1. The stories connect launch, journey, arrival, discoveries and present-day status.

How it works

One real-date simulation clock runs the whole app. Planet and Moon positions are calculated with astronomy-engine within the supported date range. Solid bodies use true-scale sizes and distances; screen-size machine markers are not to scale.

Hardware appears according to its launch date. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 use cached NASA/JPL Horizons trajectories. Ingenuity’s interplanetary journey uses the trajectory of Mars 2020, which carried it to Mars. Not a reconstruction of its helicopter flights. Apollo, Viking 1 and Opportunity journeys use explicitly labelled simplified paths between sourced milestones.

Published coordinates anchor Moon and Mars sites to rotating surfaces. Where available, orbital imagery and elevation data add real surface detail. Opportunity’s final-location coordinates and Ingenuity’s final-airfield coordinates are not supplied in the cached dataset; their recorded landing sites are not presented as confirmed final positions.

NASA 3D Resources supplies models for Voyager, Ingenuity, Opportunity, Viking and the Apollo Lunar Module. The lunar rovers and Apollo 11 reflector use clearly identified simplified models based on sourced dimensions. The complete lunar-module model is not a reconstruction of only the descent stage remaining on the Moon.

Selecting hardware opens a card with sourced facts, status information and credited NASA archival photographs. These photographs are historical records, not images captured from the simulation.

All seven tours use the same tour engine as Pale Dot’s original “Begin at Earth” journey. Left Behind is a layer within the existing universe, not a separate app or mode.

Voyager 1’s “One Last Look” uses dated positions for an illustrative Sunward view on 14 February 1990, alongside NASA’s Pale Blue Dot and Family Portrait photographs. It does not claim to reproduce measured spacecraft attitude. A screen-pixel comparison explains NASA’s reported image size: Earth occupied about 0.12 pixel in Voyager’s photograph.

A simulated signal race compares light-travel times to the seven tour groups using distances calculated at send time. Progress persists on the device independently of the simulation clock. Nothing is actually transmitted, and an earliest possible reply time does not promise a spacecraft response.

Measurements distinguish NASA-reported values, calculations, estimates and simplified paths. Nothing is presented as live telemetry.

How NASA data is used

Cached JPL Horizons data supplies supported spacecraft positions and derived measurements. Astronomy Engine supplies calculated planetary and Moon positions; flights without suitable cached trajectory data use labelled simplified paths.

The NASA Image and Video Library and JPL Photojournal supply archival photographs. Moon Trek, Mars Trek, NASA GIBS and mission elevation datasets provide surface imagery and terrain where available. Sources include LRO/LOLA, MGS/MOLA, LROC, HiRISE, MESSENGER and Dawn, alongside NOAA Earth relief and contributions distributed through USGS, DLR and other credited providers.

NASA 3D Resources supplies the listed spacecraft models. NASA mission pages, NSSDCA and other credited sources support hardware facts, dates, dimensions and published coordinates. Facts and source links are stored in public/left-behind/hardware.json. Data was retrieved during the event and saved as static files; the Left Behind experience does not call NASA services during exploration.

Benefits

Students often encounter spacecraft as lists of facts. Left Behind connects those facts to place, time, scale and distance. It makes the contrast between lunar hardware, Mars missions and interstellar probes explorable, and turns communication delay into an experience students can follow.

The web experience is freely accessible and designed for phones as well as larger screens, with translated content for seven locale options. Guided tours provide a structured introduction, while ordinary exploration lets students follow their own curiosity.

Intended impact

Left Behind aims to help students understand what discarded or inactive equipment still tells us about exploration. It connects machines to their discoveries, distinguishes equipment that is silent from instruments still used or spacecraft still communicating, and encourages students to inspect the evidence behind each story.

It is intended for classroom discussion and independent exploration, making scale, distance and the limits of communication more concrete. These are intended educational benefits, not claims of measured learning outcomes.

Tools

React, TypeScript, React Three Fiber and three.js; astronomy-engine; TanStack Start; Tailwind CSS; and Lovable. NASA data was fetched during the event and cached as static files. CREDITS.md records dependencies, fonts, datasets, imagery, models and their stated licences or usage guidance.

Creativity

The stories share one true-scale universe and one clock. Students can move from hardware on the Moon to probes in interstellar space without switching experiences. Guided narration, archival evidence, dated exploration and simulated light-travel time connect abandoned equipment to the knowledge it left us.

The final Voyager 1 sequence brings those ideas together: after following the spacecraft away from Earth, students encounter NASA’s archival view of our planet occupying a fraction of an image pixel.

Factors considered

We prioritised scientific accuracy, clear sourcing and accessibility for students aged 11–18. Real trajectories and published coordinates are used where available; simplified paths, illustrative viewpoints and missing data are identified rather than presented as measurements. Screen-size markers keep true-scale hardware findable without enlarging the machines themselves.

Left Behind stays within Pale Dot’s existing universe, preserving ordinary exploration and the original tour. Data is cached to avoid depending on NASA services during use, and feature data loads after the scene. Phone-friendly controls, translated content, keyboard access and reduced-motion support informed the design.

External assets retain their credits and rights, AI assistance is disclosed, and no NASA endorsement is implied. Physical-device performance and uninterrupted camera smoothness remain to be fully verified.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence) tools

Lovable was used to write code from my prompts. I directed the experience and reviewed and tested the implementation. Claude assisted with research, including compiling sourced hardware facts, planning and debugging. AI assistance also supported writing, editing and translation.

The project documents this assistance in HACKATHON.md and provenance comments in event-created feature files. NASA data and archival imagery were retrieved from credited sources, not generated by AI. No AI-generated imagery is used in the explorer. Archival photographs, external maps and models retain their respective credits and rights; they are not all claimed to be NASA-owned.

What existed before the event

Pale Dot existed before the hackathon. Left Behind, the shared real-date clock, true-scale corrections and the event’s surface, navigation and interface work were built during NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, 14–15 November.

The last commit before the event is the last commit dated before 14 November 2026, 09:00 GMT in the repo history. Repository history and HACKATHON.md document the event work and changes to the pre-existing app:

https://github.com/darthdens/paledot

Comparison against the recorded pre-event baseline:

https://github.com/darthdens/paledot/compare/c76c475...main

Repository code is licensed under Apache License 2.0. External assets and dependencies retain their own rights. The Pale Dot name and logo are excluded from the code licence. No NASA endorsement is implied.

What's next

Potential additions include Pioneer 10 and 11, Mars landers’ heat shields and parachutes, classroom worksheets, and further languages. These are future ideas, not submitted features.
